sources.title: The Rihla ("A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling") -- dictated by Ibn Battuta himself to the scribe Ibn Juzayy upon his return to Morocco, c. 1355. Historians note some later passages (particularly on China) may include secondhand or embellished material, a known limitation of the source.

Ross E. Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta: A Muslim Traveler of the 14th Century (1986; rev. ed. 2005) -- scholarly cross-referencing of Rihla claims against independent regional records; explicitly assesses the China chapters as the least reliable (confused chronology, a description of Chinese ceramics judged inaccurate) and the Maldives material as comparatively more credible, since no competing period source exists to contradict it either

Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi -- an independent contemporary chronicle by a Nadim (companion) actually present at Muhammad bin Tughluq's court, establishing the court's well-documented volatility toward officials/scholars generally. Note: Barani is independently known to have deliberately omitted a specific incriminating episode about Tughluq out of deference to his successor -- used here only as evidence the source is politically constrained, not as a clean, unbiased corroboration of every Ibn Battuta claim about that court

curiosity.rationale: The Rihla documents roughly three decades of continuous travel across the Islamic world and beyond (North and West Africa, the Middle East, Central and South Asia, and claimed travel to China), with sustained attention throughout to local governance, food, customs, and religious practice -- his own dictated account, though the latest sections carry acknowledged reliability caveats.

risk_tolerance.rationale: Left Morocco at 21 for the Hajj pilgrimage and, per his own account, simply continued rather than returning home, eventually surviving shipwrecks, robbery, and serious illness across the journey -- documented in the Rihla's own narrative, corroborated in outline by the independently verifiable route through regions with other contemporary records.

adaptability.rationale: [NEW_EVIDENCE, this session] A more specific instance now sharpens the generic 'different courts' framing: at Tughluq's court -- independently established as genuinely volatile toward officials via Barani's contemporary chronicle, not just Ibn Battuta's own account -- he carried two specific, separately-noted liabilities (marriage to the daughter of an executed rebel official; friendship with a Sufi who avoided political entanglement, itself viewed with suspicion), yet continued his judicial career there without the fate that befell others at that same court. Kept at strong_inference, not documented -- Barani's chronicle is independently confirmed to have politically self-censored other episodes about this same court, so it corroborates the court's general danger, not this specific personal episode's every detail.

autonomy_need.rationale: Sustained an independently self-directed, decades-long itinerary with no single sponsoring institution driving the overall journey (individual legs were sometimes patronized by local rulers), inferred from the documented absence of any single continuous authority directing his travels.

cross_domain_range.rationale: Functioned across trade, diplomacy, religious scholarship, and formal legal judgeship in the course of his travels, inferred from the documented variety of roles the Rihla describes him occupying in different regions.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: Repeatedly secured patronage, appointments, or safe passage by presenting his scholarly credentials to local rulers upon arrival in new courts, inferred from the recurring pattern described across multiple different stops in the Rihla.

persistence.rationale: Continued traveling for roughly three decades despite documented setbacks (shipwreck losing his possessions near the Maldives, robbery in India), inferred from the sustained continuation of the journey across those setbacks rather than an early return home.

social_assertiveness.rationale: Repeatedly sought and gained direct audiences with reigning sultans and rulers across many distinct courts, inferred from the consistency of this pattern throughout the Rihla's account of his travels.

achievement_drive.rationale: Continued extending his travels well beyond the original pilgrimage purpose for decades, inferred as sustained ambition toward an increasingly larger goal (eventually visiting the majority of the known Islamic world) rather than one bounded task.

detail_orientation.rationale: The Rihla records specific, granular observations of local legal practice, currency, and customs across dozens of distinct locations, inferred as requiring habitual close observation from the documented density of detail in the surviving text.

collaboration.rationale: Frequently traveled and worked within caravans, embassies, and court retinues rather than alone, a genuinely moderate signal inferred from the documented social structure of his travel throughout the Rihla.

leadership_drive.rationale: Held appointed judicial authority (as qadi) rather than pursuing political rule, inferred as a moderate rather than high leadership drive from the ceiling of the formal roles the Rihla documents him holding.

impact_motivation.rationale: His stated purposes throughout blend religious duty, scholarly interest, and personal advancement rather than a single clear external-impact goal, inferred as a genuinely mixed signal from the documented range of his stated motivations across the text.

planning_orientation.rationale: The Rihla repeatedly describes decisions made opportunistically upon arrival in a new place rather than a planned itinerary set in advance, an honest lower score reflecting the documented improvisational character of the journey rather than a gap in the source.

discipline.rationale: Maintained religious scholarly practice and observance across the entire journey per the Rihla's own account, inferred as evidence of sustained personal discipline amid highly variable circumstances.

independent_thinking.rationale: Chose an unconventional life path (indefinite continued travel rather than the expected return home after pilgrimage) departing sharply from the typical trajectory of a young North African scholar of his class, inferred from the documented divergence of his actual choices from social expectation.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: The Rihla generally describes seeking accommodation with local rulers and customs rather than confrontation, an honest moderate-to-low score reflecting the documented diplomatic, adaptive tone of his interactions across the text.

resourcefulness.rationale: Recovered from the documented loss of his possessions and position after the Maldives shipwreck by resuming his scholarly/judicial career at his next stop, inferred as resourceful recovery from the account's own description of that setback and his continued travel afterward.

mastery_orientation.rationale: Held progressively more senior judicial appointments across his later travels (culminating in the Delhi and Maldives qadi positions), inferred as accumulating recognized expertise over time from the documented trajectory of his roles.

creative_originality.rationale: His choice to indefinitely extend a religious pilgrimage into a decades-long circuit of the Islamic world had no clear precedent among his contemporaries, inferred as a genuinely novel life approach from the documented absence of comparable cases in the period's sources.

deep_focus.rationale: The Rihla's episodic, place-to-place structure suggests a pattern of broad engagement across many settings rather than sustained deep absorption in any single pursuit, an honest moderate-to-low score reflecting the documented breadth-over-depth character of his travels.

provenance.notes: Roster-1000 session 11: medieval-era + North Africa diversity pick, explorer occupation (previously only Ernest Shackleton). Sourced from his own dictated Rihla -- a rare case of direct first-person medieval travel narrative -- but confidence is held at a genuinely moderate ceiling (0.62 max) reflecting the real, acknowledged historiographical caveat that some later passages (especially on China) may include secondhand or embellished material; several rows honestly scored low/moderate (planning_orientation 38, conflict_tolerance 48) rather than defaulting every explorer trait to a high score. Track C evidence-deepening pass (2026-09-03): added Dunn's scholarly cross-referencing (confirms China chapters are the least reliable part of the Rihla, Maldives comparatively more credible -- no row here draws on China specifically, so no existing row needed to be walked back) and Barani's independent Delhi-court chronicle. Explicitly tested whether Barani provides clean independent corroboration and found it does NOT -- Barani is independently documented to have politically self-censored a separate episode about the same court, so it corroborates general court volatility only, not Ibn Battuta's specific personal account. 1 row upgraded (adaptability) using a genuinely more specific version of an already-scored fact, not a new independent witness to a new episode. This is the expected, honest outcome for this candidate: real, disclosed improvement within a structural ceiling that further ordinary source-mining is unlikely to lift, since the single-dictated-narrative problem is not a research-effort problem.
